title: The seven seas
hookLine: flowers that never withered, and seas called home by thought
carry: the holy rivers can come to where you are
last: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT.

cards: Shabari's work isn't finished when Rama arrives. She has one more thing to do: show him the place. Here Valmiki's Shabari is less a hostess than a guide, walking the brothers through the forest her teachers left behind.
It's the tour an old caretaker gives before handing over a house: this is where the light comes in, this door sticks, this is the room where we used to sing. She isn't showing off.
She's making sure the place is remembered properly.

teach.b: She shows them Matanga's forest. Here, she says, is the altar where my teachers made their offerings. And look: the flowers they offered haven't withered, after all these years.
And here is a place they called the seven seas. When the old sages grew too frail to travel to the sacred waters, they called the seven seas here by the power of their thought.
Hold on to that, because Hindus still do a version of it.

teach.h: TIRTHA: WHERE THE SACRED FEELS CLOSE.
teach.b: A holy bathing place is called a tirtha, a crossing, a place where the sacred feels close, and pilgrims travel for days to bathe in the Ganga. But most people can't go every day.
So in many pujas, a pot of water is filled and the holy rivers are asked to come into it: Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari, Sarasvati, Narmada, Sindhu, Kaveri, be present in this water.
It's the same hope as the old sages': the sacred can come to where you are. Then Shabari asks Rama's leave. I want to leave this body, she says, and go to the sages I served.
Rama gives it. She enters a fire, rises from it radiant, and goes to the world where her teachers are. She had waited for one meeting; when it came, her work was done.

teach.h: SHE RISES; THE FOREST BOOK ENDS.
teach.b: And here, beside Lake Pampa, the Aranya Kanda, the forest book, ends. It began among sages and ends with a sage's student. Tomorrow a new book opens, by a lake in spring, and someone is about to come down a mountain.

how: Shabari's hermitage is remembered at sites near Pampa, by Hampi in Karnataka. In many home and temple pujas, a verse invites the seven holy rivers into the water pot (kalasha), so the sacred waters come to the worshiper.

games.q: Nani's knees are bad and she can't make the pilgrimage this year. she's sad. what's a real Hindu answer?
o: tell her a puja at home is never the same thing.
do what Matanga's sages did: call the holy waters home in a puja.
tell her holy places don't really matter anyway.
games.why: When Matanga's sages were too old to travel, they called the seven seas to them. Families still call the sacred rivers into a pot of water at home.

practice: Fill a cup with water and hold it in both hands. If you pray, do what many Hindus do: name the holy rivers and ask them to be present, or simply say Ganga, once, softly.

If you don't pray, think of a place that once felt holy to you, and let it come here. Breathe slowly, then pour the water with care onto a plant, the way many families give offered water back to the earth.

wordCard.voice: Shabari. She shows Rama her teachers' forest, then leaves this world through fire, and the forest book ends.

orig.note: Sanskrit tīrtha: a ford, a crossing place; a holy place or holy water where the sacred is near.

carryVoice: Your line: the holy rivers can come to where you are. Shabari's long wait ended in one meeting. See you tomorrow.
